title: Dijkstra's shortest path
overview: When edges have weights, BFS levels are no longer shortest distances. Dijkstra's algorithm fixes this by always expanding the node with the smallest known distance, using a min-priority queue. The module builds a naive queue version first, then the optimized priority-queue version, and practises it on GFG, CSES and LeetCode.

concepts.explain: `dis[v]` = best cost found so far from the source; start with `INT_MAX` (infinity) and `dis[src] = 0`.
For an edge `u → v` with weight `w`: if `dis[u] + w < dis[v]`, update `dis[v]` and push `v` again.
concepts.snippet: if(d + w < dis[v]){ dis[v] = d + w; pq.push({dis[v], v}); }

concepts.explain: `priority_queue<pair<int,int>, vector<pair<int,int>>, greater<pair<int,int>>>` pops the smallest pair; pairs compare by `first`, so store `{distance, node}`.
A plain queue works but may re-process nodes many times. The priority queue processes the closest node first, giving O((V + E) log V).
Dijkstra assumes a node's distance is final once popped as the smallest; a negative edge can break that. Use Bellman-Ford then.
Building Roads: the number of new roads needed is (components − 1); connect one representative of each piece to the next.

files.title: Min-heap of pairs
files.what: Pushes four pairs into a min-priority queue and prints the top, showing that pairs are ordered by their first value.
steps: Declare the queue with `greater<pair<int,int>>` so the smallest comes out first.
files.output_note: It prints `1 4`: the pair with the smallest first value. Without `greater` it would print `10 2`.

check.q: Why does Dijkstra push `{distance, node}` and not `{node, distance}`?
check.a: Pairs compare by `first`, and we want the smallest distance on top.

files.title: Dijkstra with a plain queue
files.what: Relaxes edges using an ordinary FIFO queue of `{node, distance}` pairs.
steps: For each `(child_node, child_dist)`: if `par_dist + child_dist < dis[child_node]`, update and push the child.
Nodes can enter the queue many times; the loop ends when nothing improves.
files.complexity: Worst case exponential-ish re-processing; fine for tiny graphs
files.input_note: `n e`, then e lines `a b w` (undirected). Source is node 0.
files.output_note: The real output is **empty**: the program never prints the distances (see watch out). The distances it computes are 0, 7, 3, 9.
files.watch_out: After `dijkstra(0)` the code resets `dis` to `INT_MAX` a second time instead of printing it - a copy-paste slip. Replace the second loop with `cout << i << "->" << dis[i] << endl;`.

check.q: Why is the plain-queue version slower?
check.a: It may pop a node with an outdated larger distance and re-relax its edges many times.

files.title: Dijkstra with a priority queue
files.what: The standard Dijkstra: a min-heap always gives the closest unfinished node.
steps: Relax every edge from `par_node`, pushing `{dis[child], child}` when improved.
files.complexity: Time O((V + E) log V) · Space O(V + E)
files.input_note: `n e`, then e lines `a b w`. The direct edge 0-1 costs 10, but 0-2-1 costs 3 + 4 = 7.
files.output_note: `1->7` shows Dijkstra chose the cheaper two-edge path over the direct edge; `3->9` is 0-2-1-3.
files.watch_out: Nodes can be popped with an outdated distance; adding `if (par_dist > dis[par_node]) continue;` skips that extra work.

check.q: Why would BFS give the wrong answer for node 1 here?
check.a: BFS counts edges, so it would pick the direct 1-edge path costing 10.

files.title: GFG - Implementing Dijkstra
files.what: The same priority-queue Dijkstra as a function that takes the adjacency list and returns the distance vector.
steps: Push `{0, src}` and relax edges as usual.
files.complexity: Time O((V + E) log V) · Space O(V)
files.input_note: Driver format: `V E`, E lines `a b w`, then `src`. Same graph as the lesson.

check.q: What does `dist[x]` stay at if x is unreachable?

files.title: LeetCode 743 - Network Delay Time
files.what: Run Dijkstra from `k` on a directed graph; the answer is the largest distance, or -1 if some node is unreachable.
steps: Build directed edges `a → b` with time `c` (nodes are 1-based, arrays have room).
Otherwise return the maximum `dis[i]`: the moment the last node hears the signal.
files.complexity: Time O((V + E) log V) · Space O(V + E)
files.input_note: Driver format: cases; each `m n k` then m lines `u v w`. Case 1 is LeetCode example 1; case 2 starts at node 2 with only the edge 1→2.
files.output_note: `2` (expected answer of example 1) and `-1` (from node 2 the signal cannot reach node 1).

check.q: Why the maximum distance and not the sum?
check.a: The signal travels to all nodes at the same time; we wait until the farthest one receives it.

files.title: GFG - Detect cycle (BFS version)

problem.name: GFG - Detect cycle in an undirected graph

files.what: Tries the Module 6 parent rule with BFS, storing `{node, parent}` pairs in the queue.
steps: `isCycle` loops over all nodes and starts BFS on unvisited ones.
The queue holds `{child, curr}` so each node knows its parent.
A visited neighbour that is not the parent should mean a cycle.
files.input_note: Driver format: cases; each `V E` then E edges. A triangle, then a simple path.
files.output_note: The real output is a compile error: `'V' was not declared`. With both fixes below it would print `true` then `false`.
files.watch_out: Two mistakes. (1) `vector<bool> vis(V, false)` uses `V`, which does not exist here; use `n`. (2) The check uses the function argument `parent` (always -1) instead of the popped node's parent `par`, so every edge back to a parent would look like a cycle. Write `if (vis[child] && par != child)`.

check.q: Which parent must be compared in the BFS version?
check.a: The parent of the node just popped from the queue (`par`), stored alongside it.

files.title: CSES 1666 - Building Roads
files.what: Counts components with DFS and joins each component's first node to the next one's; k = components − 1 new roads.
steps: Loop over nodes; each unvisited node starts a DFS and its number is saved in `components`.
files.complexity: Time O(n + m) · Space O(n + m)
files.input_note: The task's sample: 4 cities, roads 1-2 and 3-4.
files.output_note: The real run **crashes** (status is an access-violation code) and prints nothing. The intended output is `1` then `2 3` (or any valid pair like `1 3`).
files.watch_out: Cities are numbered 1..n, but `adj` has size `n`, so `adj[n]` is out of range. Fix: `vector<vector<int>> adj(n + 1)`, `vis(n + 1)`, loop `i` from 1 to n and save `i` (not `i+1`).

check.a: Linking the pieces in a chain connects them all, and fewer links would leave some piece separate.

recap: Weighted shortest path, no negative edges → Dijkstra.
Relax: `if (d + w < dis[v])` update and push.
Start distances at `INT_MAX`; unreachable nodes stay there.
Watch 1-based node numbers when sizing arrays.

check_yourself.q: Why does Dijkstra fail with negative edges?
check_yourself.a: A node popped as "closest" could later get a smaller distance through a negative edge, but it is treated as final.

check_yourself.q: What is the complexity of the priority-queue version?
In `priority_queue<pair<int,int>>` without `greater`, which pair is on top?

body: In Module 2 BFS gave you shortest distances, and it was honest: every step cost the same, so the fewest steps really was the shortest way. Now look at a small map of villages where the roads have lengths in kilometres:

You are at village 0 and want to reach village 1. There is a direct road and it is 10 km. BFS would stop there and say "one road, done". But go 0 -> 2 -> 1 instead and you pay 3 + 4 = 7 km. Two roads, and still shorter.

That is the whole problem of this module. **Until now a step cost 1, so counting steps was the same as measuring distance. Here each edge carries its own weight, and the cheapest route is often not the one with the fewest edges.** BFS levels are simply the wrong answer.

The slow way out is to list every route from 0 to 1, add up the kilometres of each one, and keep the smallest. On a country with 100000 roads the number of routes is beyond counting, so that idea dies immediately.

Dijkstra's answer is patient and simple. Keep one number per village: the cheapest distance you know so far, starting at 0 for home and "unknown" for everyone else. Then repeat one move: **take the nearest village you have not finished yet, and for each road leaving it, check whether going through it makes a neighbour cheaper.** That check is called relaxing the edge. Finish the nearest one first, every time.
Run it on the map above, starting at 0. A dash means "no route known yet". Each row is the table after one village has been finished:
intro.trace:
village     0    1    2    3
start       0    -    -    -
finish 0    0   10    3    -
finish 2    0    7    3   11
finish 1    0    7    3    9
finish 3    0    7    3    9

body: Follow row three. Village 2 was the nearest unfinished one at 3 km, so it goes first, and its road to 1 costs 4. That gives 3 + 4 = 7, which beats the 10 already written down, so 10 is crossed out and 7 is written in. Village 3 improves twice in the same way: 11 through village 2, then 9 through village 1. Nothing later improves them, because every remaining village is already further away than they are.

The one tool you need is the min-priority queue from Data Structures Module 23. Push `{distance, node}` pairs; pairs compare by their first value, so the smallest distance is always on top, and "the nearest unfinished village" costs one `pq.top()`:
**A second example.** Make every road 1 km long and Dijkstra gives exactly the BFS levels back: BFS is the special case where all weights are equal.

**A third example.** In Network Delay Time a signal starts at one computer and each cable takes some milliseconds. Dijkstra gives the moment each computer hears it; the answer is the largest of those numbers, because you wait for the last one. Any computer still at infinity was never reached, and the answer is -1.

**Where it breaks.** Dijkstra rests on one promise: once a village is the nearest unfinished one, its distance is final. That promise holds only while every weight is zero or more. **A negative edge can make a finished village cheaper later, and then the promise is a lie** - so Dijkstra is not allowed on graphs with negative weights. Module 9 handles that case.

With the priority queue the cost is O((V + E) log V), which is fast enough for the judges. The programs below build it twice: first with a plain queue, so you can see why re-processing hurts, then the real version, and then the same code on GFG, LeetCode and CSES.

walkthrough.heading: Watch it happen: Dijkstra across the five roads
body: The map is the one at the top of the page, in kilometres, and the run starts at village 0. A dash means no route is known yet, and a `*` means that village is finished - its number can never change again. Watch the 10 under village 1: it does not survive.
walkthrough.frames_title: Press the arrows to finish one village at a time

frames.label: Home costs nothing, so `dis[0] = 0` and everyone else is unknown. The priority queue holds one pair, `{0, 0}`.
Village 0 is the nearest unfinished one, so it is taken and finished. Both roads leaving it are relaxed: 1 becomes 10, and 2 becomes 3.

Which village next? Not 1, even though there is a direct road to it. Compare the unfinished numbers: 3 is smaller than 10, so village 2 is the nearest and goes next. This one choice is the whole algorithm.
Finish village 2 and relax its roads. 3 + 4 = 7 beats the 10 already written for village 1, so the 10 is crossed out. 3 + 8 = 11 gives village 3 its first number.
Now 7 is the smallest unfinished number, so village 1 is finished. Its road to 3 costs 2, and 7 + 2 = 9 beats the 11, so village 3 improves a second time.
Village 3 is the last one left, at 9. Relaxing its roads changes nothing: 9 + 2 is not better than 7, and 9 + 8 is not better than 3. Everything is finished.
frames.art:
10
    0---------1
    |       / |
  3 |    4/   | 2
    |   /     |
    2---------3
        8

node     0    1    2    3
dis      0    7    3    9
done     *    *    *    *
     nothing improves, queue empties

frames.label: The queue is empty and the row is the answer. Village 1 costs 7, by going 0 -> 2 -> 1: two roads, and cheaper than the single 10 km road. That is exactly the case where BFS levels would have lied to you.
